claims.text: Polycrystalline refractory high-entropy alloys can serve as structural materials for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed refractory HEAs are low-activation materials.
Tailoring grain size distribution and precipitate architecture enhances the strength of refractory HEAs.
Tailoring grain size distribution and precipitate architecture enhances the radiation resistance of refractory HEAs.
An average grain size of 1–10 μm is an appropriate target for enhancing strength and radiation resistance.
A precipitate volume fraction of 0.1–0.5 is an appropriate target for enhancing strength and radiation resistance.
The relevant fusion-reactor service environment spans 500–1000 °C under irradiation.
The tailored microstructure reduces the formation of radiation-induced defects.
The tailored microstructure improves grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced radiation-induced defect formation and improved grain-boundary cohesion increase strength and radiation resistance.
The proposed HEAs will exhibit a 20–50% increase in yield strength relative to traditional fusion materials such as stainless steel or tungsten.
The proposed HEAs will exhibit a 10–30% reduction in radiation-induced swelling relative to traditional fusion materials such as stainless steel or tungsten.
Grain size distribution and precipitate architecture must be optimized to obtain the desired properties.
Powder metallurgy or additive manufacturing can provide the desired HEA microstructure.
The exact relationship among grain size distribution, precipitate architecture, and radiation resistance is not fully understood.
